topic: Multi-intent task decomposition for LLM tool and skill routing
name: MasRouter / Router-R1
description: Two 2025 research efforts that push LLM routing beyond RouteLLM's single binary strong-vs-weak gate. MasRouter (arXiv:2502.11133, ACL 2025, Yue et al.) formalizes Multi-Agent System Routing (MASR): given a query it jointly decides the collaboration topology (chain/tree/debate), the number and roles of agents, and which LLM backbone serves each role, via a cascaded controller (variational collaboration-mode determiner + structured-cascade role allocator + multinomial LLM router) trained by policy-gradient RL on a utility-minus-cost objective. Router-R1 (arXiv:2506.09033, NeurIPS 2025, Zhang/Feng/You, UIUC) instantiates the router itself as a policy LLM that interleaves <think> reasoning with <route> actions, performing multi-round routing AND aggregation as a sequential decision process; it is RL-trained (GRPO, built on veRL/Search-R1) with a rule-based reward (format + outcome + cost). Both extend binary routing toward multi-intent / multi-agent decisions: MasRouter plans a whole MAS up front; Router-R1 routes adaptively across multiple LLMs over several rounds, fusing their answers.
decomposition_method: MasRouter: implicit, learned decomposition into agent roles — a structured probabilistic cascade (role allocator) generates an ordered set of agent roles (e.g., programmer then tester) conditioned on the query and chosen topology; it does not split the prompt into text sub-tasks but into role/agent slots. Router-R1: LLM-prompted (RL-trained) — the policy LLM itself decides, round by round, what sub-queries to issue to which model via <think>/<route> tokens; no separate splitter. Both are best characterized as learned/RL-trained rather than parser- or grammar-based. [uncertain]
decomposition_granularity: MasRouter: agent/role unit (each sub-task = one agent role in the assembled MAS). Router-R1: sub-query / route-call unit (each routed turn is a model invocation with its own query). Neither uses sentence/clause-level text splitting. [uncertain]
ordering_strategy: MasRouter: topology-determined — the variational collaboration-mode determiner picks a topology (chain = sequential, tree, debate) and the role cascade imposes dependency order (e.g., programmer before tester); order is fixed once the MAS is constructed before execution. Router-R1: dynamic (mid-chain) — multi-round routing decides each next route action online based on accumulated context, so ordering is sequential but adaptively (re-)planned each round rather than fixed up front.
decomposition_validation: Neither performs an explicit AOP-style solvability/completeness/non-redundancy check before dispatch. MasRouter validates indirectly through the RL reward: the assembled MAS is executed and the utility-minus-cost outcome shapes the controller, so poor role/topology choices are penalized in training but not verified per-query at inference. Router-R1 likewise relies on the outcome + format + cost reward during RL; at inference the policy LLM self-judges whether external routing is needed (it can answer simple questions from internal knowledge) but there is no independent detector/reward-model gate validating the decomposition itself. Validation is therefore learned/implicit, not an explicit pre-dispatch verifier. [uncertain]
hierarchy_depth: MasRouter: two-level — a topology over multiple agent roles (collaboration mode containing ordered roles), effectively a small graph/tree of agents rather than a flat list. Router-R1: flat sequence of route calls (multi-round but a single reasoning chain, no nested sub-agent hierarchy). [uncertain]
router_type: MasRouter: graph planner — a cascaded controller plans the full multi-agent configuration (topology + roles + per-role LLM) up front; LLM selection modeled as a multinomial distribution. Router-R1: chain / sequential router realized as an autoregressive policy LLM that interleaves reasoning and route actions (multi-round, one route decision per turn). Together they move from single-label gating toward multi-label/graph and sequential routing.
routing_model: MasRouter: separate trained controller network (cascaded: variational latent-variable collaboration determiner + probabilistic role allocator + multinomial LLM router), optimized by policy-gradient RL — not the main answering LLM. Router-R1: RL-trained router that IS a capable LLM (policy LLM, e.g., Qwen2.5 / Llama variants), trained with GRPO; conditions only on lightweight model descriptors (price, latency, example performance) for the candidate pool. Both are RL-trained routers.
handles_ambiguity: MasRouter: best-effort learned configuration — for ambiguous/complex queries the complexity function increases the number of agents and may select richer topologies (debate/tree) to hedge, but there is no clarification request or abstention; the controller commits to its sampled MAS. Router-R1: best-effort multi-round resolution — when uncertain it can issue additional route calls to multiple models and aggregate, and it learns to decide whether external routing is needed at all; still no user-facing clarification or explicit abstain. Neither uses POMDP/clarification-based disambiguation. [uncertain]
fallback_behavior: MasRouter: route to general LLM / fall back to single-agent or smaller configuration — the cost-aware controller can assign a simple query to a minimal MAS (effectively one agent / one model); no human escalation or hard abort described. Router-R1: route to general LLM (internal knowledge) — for simple questions the policy LLM answers directly without routing; for failures it can issue further route rounds. Neither documents an explicit error/abort or human-escalation path. [uncertain]
skill_pool_scale_and_retrieval: Routing pool here is a set of LLM backbones, not a large skill/tool registry. MasRouter: LLM selection over a modest candidate set of model backbones modeled as a multinomial; shown to generalize inductively to unseen backbones. Router-R1: candidate models described by compact descriptors (pricing, latency, example performance) injected into context, enabling zero-shot generalization to unseen models. Neither targets hundreds/thousands of skills via embedding retrieval or retrieve-then-rerank; scaling is over a handful-to-dozens of models, not a skill pool. [uncertain]
router_agent_asymmetry: Not a focus. In MasRouter the controller decides backbones for agents but agents execute with their own prompts; in Router-R1 the router LLM holds the evolving context while routed models see only the issued sub-query, an implicit asymmetry, but neither frames routing around full-skill-body-vs-name access the way SkillRouter does. [uncertain]
execution_pattern: MasRouter: DAG / topology-defined multi-agent execution — chain (sequential), tree, or debate among assigned agents, run after the MAS is constructed. Router-R1: sequential ReAct-style loop — interleaved think/route turns where each routed model response is folded back into context before the next route, ending in an aggregated answer.
parallel_vs_concurrent: MasRouter: depends on chosen topology — chain is sequential, debate/tree allow multiple agents whose contributions may be combined, but the paper does not emphasize parallel-API-call batching vs. true concurrency. Router-R1: inherently sequential (each route round depends on prior responses); not parallel/concurrent. [uncertain]
dependency_detection: MasRouter: explicit from the planned topology + role cascade — role dependencies (e.g., programmer before tester) and the selected collaboration mode encode which agents feed which, learned by the controller. Router-R1: implicit/dynamic — the policy LLM decides dependencies on the fly by reasoning about what information it still needs before the next route; no separate dependency classifier. [uncertain]
result_aggregation: MasRouter: topology-defined aggregation — outputs of collaborating agents are combined per the collaboration mode (e.g., debate consensus, chain hand-off to a final role); a final agent typically produces the answer. Router-R1: LLM aggregation — the policy LLM integrates each routed model's response into its evolving context and produces the final answer (multi-round routing AND aggregation is the named contribution).
mid_chain_feedback: MasRouter: none (hard plan up front) — routing decisions (topology, roles, backbones) are fixed before inference begins, which follow-up work explicitly notes prevents state-dependent rescheduling as the trajectory unfolds. Router-R1: hard / dynamic re-planning — each round's route decision is conditioned on prior responses, so later actions adapt to earlier results (its key advantage over fixed-plan routers like MasRouter).
benchmark_name: MasRouter: MMLU, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, MBPP (five reasoning/code benchmarks; compared vs RouterDC, AgentPrune, AFlow, GPTSwarm). Router-R1: seven QA benchmarks — NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA (general) and HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, Musique, Bamboogle (multi-hop); trained on NQ+HotpotQA (14K samples).
multi_intent_coverage: MasRouter: mixed — multi-agent collaboration with role dependencies covers compound reasoning, but benchmarks are standard single-answer tasks rather than explicitly compound multi-intent prompts. Router-R1: sequential multi-intent via multi-hop QA — multi-hop benchmarks require chaining dependent sub-queries, and Router-R1 makes more route calls on harder multi-hop tasks; this is dependent/sequential multi-intent rather than parallel independent intents. [uncertain]
accuracy_metric: MasRouter: outcome-based task accuracy / pass@1 (code) and accuracy (reasoning), reported jointly with cost/overhead reduction (e.g., +1.8 on MBPP, up to 52.07% overhead cut on HumanEval, 3.51% avg gain over RouterDC). Router-R1: outcome-based Exact Match (EM) as primary (best avg EM ~0.409 Llama / ~0.416 Qwen), with F1 selectable as the reward metric; evaluated on final-answer correctness, not intermediate process supervision.
clarification_capability: Not measured by either. Neither MasRouter nor Router-R1 models when-to-ask vs. when-to-answer or generates clarification questions; Router-R1 does decide when external routing is unnecessary, but this is answer-vs-route, not user clarification. [uncertain]
process_vs_outcome_eval: Both are outcome-only — MasRouter optimizes/evaluates on final task success vs. cost; Router-R1's reward and metrics (EM/F1) score the final answer plus a format reward, with no intermediate process-reward model scoring each routing step.
eval_stability: MasRouter: reproducible offline benchmarks (MMLU/GSM8K/MATH/HumanEval/MBPP) with released code, though numbers depend on the external LLM APIs used as backbones. Router-R1: standard QA datasets with released code/weights, but reported accuracy depends on the live LLM API pool routed to (pricing/behavior of those models can drift). Neither uses a StableToolBench-style cached virtual API server. [uncertain]
integration_pattern: MasRouter: plug-and-play standalone routing/controller layer that integrates with mainstream MAS frameworks (GPTSwarm/AFlow-style) to assign topology/roles/backbones before execution. Router-R1: standalone RL-trained router service/model (built on veRL/Search-R1); the LLM routing pool is configured via a route_service module (check_llm_name + API_PRICE_1M_TOKENS dict). Both sit at the application layer in front of the executing LLMs.
routing_layer: application-layer for both — MasRouter is an orchestration/controller tier configuring a MAS; Router-R1 is an application-level policy LLM that calls model APIs. Neither pushes routing into the inference engine (no Envoy/ext_proc-style inference-layer routing). [uncertain]
latency_overhead: MasRouter: adds a controller forward pass to plan the MAS, but the paper emphasizes net savings — 40.22%-43.78% lower inference overhead vs AFlow and up to ~52% lower cost vs SOTA, plus 69.57%-83.51% training-resource savings vs GPTSwarm/AFlow; planning overhead is small relative to MAS execution. Router-R1: incurs multi-round latency — several think/route turns and extra LLM API calls (more on hard multi-hop queries), trading latency/cost for accuracy, with the cost reward bounding excessive expensive-model use.
online_adaptation: RL-trained for both, but offline. MasRouter: policy-gradient RL on utility-vs-cost, trained offline then deployed (decisions fixed before inference; no documented production-feedback loop). Router-R1: GRPO RL training offline, deployed as a fixed policy at inference (adaptive per-query across rounds, but the policy weights are static post-training). Effectively static-after-training RL routers rather than continual online bandit learning. [uncertain]
adoption: Both open-source (with code), paper-stage research, no commercial API. MasRouter: code at github.com/yanweiyue/masrouter (ACL 2025). Router-R1: code at github.com/ulab-uiuc/Router-R1 with model weights + 14K training dataset on HuggingFace (NeurIPS 2025). Influential as research but not productized; relevant to Labmate as the RL-trained / multi-agent end of the routing design space.
